# mvgam

> **M**ulti**V**ariate (Dynamic) **G**eneralized **A**dditive **M**odels

[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/nicholasjclark/mvgam/workflows/R-CMD-check/badge.svg)](https://github.com/nicholasjclark/mvgam/actions/)
[![Coverage status](https://codecov.io/gh/nicholasjclark/mvgam/graph/badge.svg?token=RCJ2B7S0BL)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/nicholasjclark/mvgam)
[![Documentation](https://img.shields.io/badge/documentation-mvgam-orange.svg?colorB=brightgreen)](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/)
[![Methods in Ecology & Evolution](https://img.shields.io/badge/Methods%20in%20Ecology%20&%20Evolution-14,%20771–784-blue.svg)](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13974)
[![CRAN Version](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/mvgam)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=mvgam)
[![CRAN Downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/grand-total/mvgam?color=brightgreen)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=mvgam)

The `mvgam` 📦 fits Bayesian Dynamic Generalized Additive Models (DGAMs). A DGAM combines nonlinear predictor effects, latent variables and multivariate time series models in one state-space model. `mvgam` builds each model from [`brms`](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/){target="_blank"} and [`mgcv`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=mgcv){target="_blank"} components and estimates its parameters in [`Stan`](https://mc-stan.org/){target="_blank"}. The models it fits include:

* [Multivariate state-space time series models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/reference/mvgam.html){target="_blank"}
* [Vector autoregressions](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/var.html){target="_blank"}
* [Continuous-time autoregressions for irregularly sampled series](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/reference/trend_constructors.html){target="_blank"}
* [Dynamic factor models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/dfm.html){target="_blank"}
* [Hierarchical N-mixture and occupancy models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/nmix.html){target="_blank"}
* [Hierarchical generalized additive models](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2POK_FVwCHk){target="_blank"}
* [Joint species distribution models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/jsdgam.html){target="_blank"}

To choose a model, [`?mvgam_families`](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/reference/mvgam_families.html){target="_blank"} matches each response type to an observation family. [`?trend_constructors`](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/reference/trend_constructors.html){target="_blank"} describes each latent process and when it suits.

## Installation
Install the released version from `CRAN` with `install.packages("mvgam")`, or the development version with `devtools::install_github("nicholasjclark/mvgam")`. `mvgam` also needs a working installation of `Stan` through [`rstan`](https://mc-stan.org/users/interfaces/rstan){target="_blank"} or [`cmdstanr`](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/){target="_blank"}.

## Cheatsheet
[![`mvgam` usage cheatsheet](https://github.com/nicholasjclark/mvgam/raw/master/misc/mvgam_cheatsheet.png)](https://github.com/nicholasjclark/mvgam/raw/master/misc/mvgam_cheatsheet.pdf)

## A state-space model of rodent captures
The `portal_data` from [the Portal Project](https://portal.weecology.org/){target="_blank"} hold monthly counts of baited captures for four desert rodent species, with minimum temperature and a 12-month moving average of NDVI (see `?portal_data`). `mvgam_data()` checks that the data suit an observation family and plots each series:

```{r portal-data, fig.alt = "Exploratory plots of four rodent capture series"}
data(portal_data)
mvgam_data(portal_data, y = "captures", family = poisson())
```

The counts have missing values, many zeros, seasonality and autocorrelation. To test forecasts against data the model has not seen, we held out months 61 to 65:

```{r portal-split}
data_train <- subset(portal_data, time <= 60)
data_test <- subset(portal_data, time > 60 & time <= 65)
```

To estimate how temperature and vegetation drive each species' abundance, we fitted a state-space GAM. Each species takes its own intercept in the observation model. Each species' latent abundance takes its own smooth of minimum temperature, a smooth of NDVI shared by all four species and first-order autoregressive dynamics. `AR(cor = TRUE)` lets the four processes share correlated shocks:

```{r portal-fit, cache = TRUE, warning = FALSE}
mod <- mvgam(
  captures ~ series,
  trend_formula = ~ s(mintemp, k = 5, by = lv_axis()) +
    s(ndvi_ma12, k = 5) +
    AR(cor = TRUE),
  data = data_train,
  family = poisson(),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, silent = 2
)
summary(mod)
```

`conditional_effects()` plots the smooths on the scale of the latent process:

```{r portal-effects, fig.alt = "Smooth effects of minimum temperature and NDVI on each species' latent abundance"}
conditional_effects(mod)
```

`forecast()` continues each latent process through the five held-out months. The plot sets the forecasts against the held-out counts:

```{r portal-forecast, fig.alt = "Hindcasts and forecasts of rodent captures with the held-out observations"}
fc <- forecast(mod, newdata = data_test)
plot(fc)
```

`score()` and `compare_scores()` evaluate forecasts with proper scoring rules. The [forecast evaluation article](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/forecast_evaluation.html){target="_blank"} compares models by their forecasts.

Randomised quantile residuals plotted over time show any structure the model missed:

```{r portal-resid, fig.alt = "Randomised quantile residuals over time for each rodent species"}
pp_check(mod, type = "resid_ribbon_grouped", group = "series",
         x = "time", ndraws = 200)
```

## Vector autoregressions
A vector autoregression (VAR) lets each latent process depend on the lagged values of every process. To show what `mvgam` recovers from such a system, we simulated monthly counts of a prey species and its predator over ten years. Predators suppress the prey a month later. Prey in turn raise the predators a month later:

```{r var-sim}
set.seed(2025)
n_months <- 120
# Rows hold this month's processes, columns last month's
A <- rbind(prey     = c(0.6, -0.5),
           predator = c(0.4,  0.5))
z <- matrix(0, n_months, 2)
for (t in 2:n_months) {
  z[t, ] <- A %*% z[t - 1, ] + rnorm(2, sd = 0.35)
}
predator_prey <- data.frame(
  time = rep(seq_len(n_months), 2),
  series = factor(rep(c("prey", "predator"), each = n_months),
                  levels = c("prey", "predator")),
  y = rpois(2 * n_months, exp(c(2.5 + z[, 1], 1.5 + z[, 2])))
)
```

```{r var-fit, cache = TRUE, warning = FALSE}
mod_var <- mvgam(
  y ~ series,
  trend_formula = ~ VAR(),
  data = predator_prey,
  family = poisson(),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, silent = 2
)
```

`posterior_transition_matrix()` summarises the estimated coefficient matrix. Each cell gives the effect of a process last month (column) on a process this month (row):

```{r var-matrix, fig.height = 3.5, fig.width = 5, out.width = "60%", fig.alt = "Posterior transition matrix of the predator-prey VAR"}
A_post <- posterior_transition_matrix(mod_var)
plot(A_post)
```

```{r var-numbers, include = FALSE}
fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
irfs <- irf(mod_var, h = 12)
irf_summary <- summary(irfs)
prey_shock <- subset(irf_summary, shock == "prey -> predator")
pred_shock <- subset(irf_summary, shock == "predator -> prey")
fevds <- fevd(mod_var, h = 12)
fevd_summary <- summary(fevds)
fevd_12 <- subset(fevd_summary, horizon == 12)
share <- function(label) {
  sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * fevd_12$fevdQ50[fevd_12$shock == label])
}
```

The model recovered the simulated interactions. The predators' effect on the prey has a posterior mean of `r fmt(A_post$A["prey", "predator"])` against a true value of `r fmt(A["prey", 2])`. The prey's effect on the predators has a mean of `r fmt(A_post$A["predator", "prey"])` against `r fmt(A["predator", 1])`.

`irf()` traces how a shock to one process spreads through the system. A shock of one standard deviation to the prey raises the predators, whose response peaks `r prey_shock$horizon[which.max(prey_shock$irfQ50)]` months later at `r fmt(max(prey_shock$irfQ50))` on the log scale:

```{r var-irf-prey, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Impulse responses of both species to a shock to the prey"}
plot(irfs, series = 1)
```

The same shock to the predators lowers the prey, reaching `r fmt(min(pred_shock$irfQ50))` after `r pred_shock$horizon[which.min(pred_shock$irfQ50)]` months:

```{r var-irf-predator, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Impulse responses of both species to a shock to the predator"}
plot(irfs, series = 2)
```

`fevd()` splits the forecast variance of each process among the shocks that produce it. At a 12-month horizon, shocks to the predators account for `r share("predator -> prey")` of the prey's forecast variance. Shocks to the prey account for `r share("prey -> predator")` of the predators' forecast variance:

```{r var-fevd, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Forecast error variance decompositions of the predator-prey VAR"}
plot(fevds)
```

The [VAR article](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/var.html){target="_blank"} covers higher-order and hierarchical VARs.

## Describing a fitted model
A fitted model combines published methods: an observation family, a trend model, priors and a sampler. `how_to_cite()` drafts a methods paragraph for the model and lists the references for each part:

```{r cite}
how_to_cite(mod)
```

`bibtex()` writes those references to a `.bib` file. `methods_md()` writes the model as Markdown equations with a glossary of symbols and the priors, ready for a methods section or an appendix:

<details>
<summary>The equations <code>methods_md(mod)</code> writes for the rodent model</summary>

```{r methods-md, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# Nest the section headings under the README's own
cat(gsub("(^|\n)## ", "\\1#### ", methods_md(mod)))
```

</details>

## Observation families
`mvgam` began as a tool for forecasting ecological counts. Its observation families now span most of the response types met in ecological and environmental monitoring.

For continuous responses:

* `gaussian()` for real-valued data
* `student()` for real-valued data with heavy tails
* `lognormal()` and `Gamma()` for strictly positive data
* `exponential()` for waiting times
* `Beta()` for proportions on `(0, 1)`
* `tweedie()` for positive continuous data carrying an exact mass at zero, such as catch per unit effort or rainfall

For counts and binary outcomes:

* `poisson()` for equidispersed counts
* `negbinomial()` for overdispersed counts
* `beta_nb()` for counts whose tails run heavier than a negative binomial can reach
* `bernoulli()` for binary data
* `binomial()` and `beta_binomial()` for counts with a known number of trials
* `com_binomial()` for bounded counts that are under-, over- or super-dispersed relative to a binomial

A further group of families operates on *closure units*, where several rows of the data share a single latent state. `mvgam` groups the rows of a unit by their `series` and `time` values. Replicate visits to a site and the species of one assemblage then need no reshaping:

* `nmix()` for repeat counts of an unknown abundance seen with imperfect detection
* `occ()` for repeat detection and non-detection visits to a site of unknown occupancy
* `multi()` and `diri()` for compositional counts and proportions that sum within a unit
* `categ()` for a single categorical outcome per unit
* `mvn()` and `mvt()` for continuous multi-species responses with a low-rank residual covariance, the latter permitting heavier tails

`?mvgam_families` lists the full set, grouped by the kind of response each one suits. To show a `Beta` model, we simulated proportions for three series. Each series has a smooth covariate effect and its own autoregressive trend:

```{r beta-sim, fig.alt = "Exploratory plots of three simulated series of proportions"}
set.seed(100)
beta_data <- sim_mvgam(
  family = Beta(),
  n_series = 3L,
  n_timepoints = 80L,
  trend_model = AR(),
  prop_trend = 0.5
)
mvgam_data(beta_data$data_train, y = "y", family = Beta())
```

```{r beta-fit, cache = TRUE, warning = FALSE}
mod_beta <- mvgam(
  y ~ s(x, by = series, k = 6),
  trend_formula = ~ AR(p = 1),
  data = beta_data$data_train,
  newdata = beta_data$data_test,
  family = Beta(),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, silent = 2
)
```

The posterior holds an estimate of the `Beta` precision parameter $\phi$ for each series:

```{r beta-summary}
summary(mod_beta)
```

The hindcasts and forecasts of each series, against the held-out observations:

```{r beta-forecast, fig.alt = "Hindcasts and forecasts of three series of proportions"}
plot(forecast(mod_beta))
```

The [package documentation](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/){target="_blank"} covers the other uses of `mvgam`, among them dynamic and spatially varying coefficients, dynamic factors and joint species distribution models. `stancode()` and `standata()` return the `Stan` program and data of any model for users who wish to adapt it. The [`Stan` Discourse](https://discourse.mc-stan.org/){target="_blank"} is a helpful place to troubleshoot.

## Citing `mvgam` and related software
Research software is written and maintained by people whose only currency is citation. If `mvgam` contributed to an analysis, please cite it and the packages it depends on. A ⭐ on the repository is welcome too.

When using `mvgam`, please cite the following:

> Clark, N.J. and Wells, K. (2023). Dynamic Generalized Additive Models (DGAMs) for forecasting discrete ecological time series. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13974

As `mvgam` acts as an interface to `Stan`, please additionally cite:

> Carpenter B., Gelman A., Hoffman M. D., Lee D., Goodrich B., Betancourt M., Brubaker M., Guo J., Li P., and Riddell A. (2017). Stan: A probabilistic programming language. *Journal of Statistical Software*. 76(1). DOI: https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v076.i01

`how_to_cite(mod)` lists the further references for the family, trend model and sampler of a fitted model.

## Getting help
Bug reports belong on the [issue tracker](https://github.com/nicholasjclark/mvgam/issues). A minimal reproducible example makes a report fixable. Questions about model syntax, priors or interpretation are better suited to the [`mvgam` Discussion Board](https://github.com/nicholasjclark/mvgam/discussions), where an earlier thread has often covered the same ground already. The [Changelog](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/news/index.html) records what changed in each release.
